labels.text: Deﬁnition 6.1. A transitive edge set is a subset E of the edges of T such that if two edges
on a face are in E, so is the third. The set of transitive edge sets is denoted by T(T ). Given
E ∈T(T ), we refer to the edges in E as zero-edges. To stress the dependence on T we sometimes
denote a transitive edge set as (T , E) instead of E.

Deﬁnition 6.3. Let E ∈T(T ) be a transitive edge set. A face of T is degenerate if all its three
edges are zero-edges. A simplex of T is degenerate if all of its six edges are zero-edges.
Deﬁnition 6.4. We divide the transitive edge sets into the following types:
Non-degenerate: No zero-edges (there is a unique such).
Edge-degenerate: Some zero-edges, but no degenerate faces.
Face-degenerate: Some degenerate faces, but no degenerate simplices.
Simplex-degenerate: Some, but not all, simplices are degenerate.
Totally degenerate: All simplices are degenerate (there is a unique such).
Clearly, any E ∈T(T ) falls into exactly one of these types.
6.1. Decorations, Ptolemy assignments and Bruhat cocycles.
Deﬁnition 6.5. Let E ∈T(T ). A decoration is of type E if its zero-edges agree with E. A
Bruhat cocycle τ has type E if the set of long edges that are diagonal agrees with the zero-edges
of E. A Ptolemy assignment has type E if the set of edges whose Ptolemy coordinate is zero
agrees with the zero-edges of E.
Note that the one-to-one-correspondence in Theorem 4.8 preserves the type. We stress that
the type depends on the triangulation.
